questions.stem:
Figure 1 shows a sketch of parallelogram $ABCD$.
Given that $\overrightarrow{AB}=6\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}=2\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j}+8\mathbf{k}$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) find the size of angle $ABC$, giving your answer in degrees, to 2 decimal places.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Attempts the scalar product of $\pm\overrightarrow{AB}.\pm\overrightarrow{BC}$ condone slips as long as the intention is clear. Or attempts the vector product $\pm\overrightarrow{AB}\times\pm\overrightarrow{BC}$. Or attempts vector $AC$.
dM1: Attempts to use $\pm\overrightarrow{AB}.\overrightarrow{BC}=|\overrightarrow{AB}||\overrightarrow{BC}|\cos\theta$ AND proceeds to a value for $\theta$. Expect to see at least one correct attempted calculation for a modulus, e.g. $\sqrt{2^2+5^2+8^2}(=\sqrt{93})$ or $\sqrt{6^2+2^2+3^2}(=7)$. Note that we condone poor notation such as $\cos\theta=\frac{26}{7\sqrt{93}}=67.35^\circ$. Depends on the first mark. Must be an attempt to find the correct angle.
A1: $\theta=$ awrt $112.65^\circ$. Versions finishing with $\theta=$ awrt $67.35^\circ$ will normally score M1 dM1 A0. Angles given in radians also score A0 (NB $\theta=1.9661...$ or acute $1.1754...$). Allow e.g. $\theta=67.35^\circ\Rightarrow\theta=180-67.35^\circ=112.65^\circ$.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- $\overrightarrow{BA}.\overrightarrow{BC}=-6\times2+2\times5-3\times8=(-26)$ M1
- Uses $\overrightarrow{BA}.\overrightarrow{BC}=|\overrightarrow{BA}||\overrightarrow{BC}|\cos\theta\Rightarrow-26=\sqrt{49}\times\sqrt{93}\cos\theta\Rightarrow\theta=...$ dM1; $\theta=112.65^\circ$ A1
- and allow $\cos\theta=\frac{26}{7\sqrt{93}}\Rightarrow\theta=112.65$
- 1. Alternative using the vector product: M1: Attempts the vector product $\pm\overrightarrow{AB}\times\pm\overrightarrow{BC}=\pm\begin{pmatrix}6\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}\times\pm\begin{pmatrix}2\\5\\8\end{pmatrix}=\pm\begin{pmatrix}-31\\-42\\34\end{pmatrix}$ condone slips as long as the intention is clear. dM1: Attempts to use $\pm\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{BC}=|\overrightarrow{AB}||\overrightarrow{BC}|\sin\theta$ AND proceeds to a value for $\theta$. Expect to see at least one correct attempted calculation for a modulus on rhs and attempt at the modulus of the vector product For example $\sqrt{2^2+5^2+8^2}$ or $\sqrt{6^2+2^2+3^2}$ and $\sqrt{31^2+42^2+34^2}(=\sqrt{3881})$ Note that we condone poor notation such as: $\sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt{3881}}{7\sqrt{93}}=67.35^\circ$ Depends on the first mark. Must be an attempt to find the correct angle. A1: $\theta=$ awrt $112.65^\circ$ Versions finishing with $\theta=$ awrt $67.35^\circ$ will normally score M1 dM1 A0
- 2. Alternative using cosine rule: M1: Attempts $\pm\overrightarrow{AC}=\pm(\overrightarrow{AB}+\overrightarrow{BC})=\pm(8\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}+11\mathbf{k})$ condone slips and poor notation as long as the intention is clear e.g. allow $\begin{pmatrix}8\mathbf{i}\\3\mathbf{j}\\11\mathbf{k}\end{pmatrix}$ dM1: Attempts to use $AC^2=AB^2+BC^2-2AB.BC\cos\theta$ AND proceeds to a value for $\theta$ Must be an attempt to find the correct angle. A1: $\theta=$ awrt $112.65^\circ$

parts.text:
(b) Find the area of parallelogram $ABCD$, giving your answer to one decimal place.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Attempts to use $|\overrightarrow{AB}||\overrightarrow{BC}|\sin\theta$ with their $\theta$. You may see $\frac{1}{2}|\overrightarrow{AB}||\overrightarrow{BC}|\sin\theta$ found first before it is doubled. Or attempts the magnitude of their vector product e.g. $\sqrt{3881}$.

questions.stem:
With respect to a fixed origin $O$, the lines $l_1$ and $l_2$ are given by the equations
$$l_1:\quad \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\5\\4\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\5\end{pmatrix} \qquad l_2:\quad \mathbf{r}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\-5\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}4\\-3\\b\end{pmatrix}$$
where $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are scalar parameters and $b$ is a constant.

parts.text:
Prove that for all values of $b\neq 7$, the lines $l_1$ and $l_2$ are skew.
(6)
parts.mark_scheme:
$\begin{pmatrix}-1\\5\\4\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\5\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\\-5\end{pmatrix}+\mu\begin{pmatrix}4\\-3\\b\end{pmatrix}\Rightarrow -1+2\lambda=2+4\mu$ (1) $\quad 5-\lambda=-2-3\mu$ (2) $\quad 4+5\lambda=-5+\mu b$ (3)
M1: Uses equations (1) and (2) to find either $\lambda$ or $\mu$ e.g. (1)+2(2) $\Rightarrow \mu=...$ or 3(1)+4(2) $\Rightarrow \lambda=...$
dM1: Uses equations (1) and (2) to find both $\lambda$ and $\mu$
A1: $\mu=-\frac{11}{2}$ and $\lambda=-\frac{19}{2}$
ddM1: $4+5\lambda=-5+\mu b\Rightarrow 4+5\times-\frac{19}{2}=-5-\frac{11}{2}b$ or $4+5\lambda=-5+7\mu\Rightarrow 4+5\times-\frac{19}{2}=-5-\frac{11}{2}\times 7$
A1: $\Rightarrow 11b=77\Rightarrow b=7$ or obtains $-\frac{87}{2}=-\frac{87}{2}$
A1 Cso: States that when $b=7$, lines intersect or when $b\neq 7$, lines do not intersect. Lines are not parallel so when $b\neq 7$ lines are skew. *
Alternative assuming $b=7$: Uses any 2 equations to find either $\lambda$ or $\mu$ M1, both dM1, $\mu=-\frac{11}{2}$ and $\lambda=-\frac{19}{2}$ A1, checks in the 3rd equation e.g. equation 3: $4+5\left(-\frac{19}{2}\right)=-5+7\left(-\frac{11}{2}\right)=...$; equation 1: $-1+2\left(-\frac{19}{2}\right)=2+4\left(-\frac{11}{2}\right)=...$; equation 2: $5-\left(-\frac{19}{2}\right)=-2-3\left(-\frac{11}{2}\right)=...$ ddM1. Equation 3: $-\frac{87}{2}$ Equation 1: $-20$ Equation 2: $\frac{29}{2}$ A1. States that when $b=7$, lines intersect or when $b\neq 7$, lines do not intersect. Lines are not parallel so when $b\neq 7$ lines are skew. * A1 Cso.
M1: For attempting to solve equations (1) and (2) to find either $\lambda$ or $\mu$.
dM1: For attempting to solve equations (1) and (2) to find both $\lambda$ and $\mu$. Depends on the first M.
A1: $\mu=-\frac{11}{2}$ and $\lambda=-\frac{19}{2}$.
ddM1: Attempts to solve $4+5\lambda=-5+\mu b$ for their values of $\lambda$ and $\mu$. Or uses $b=7$ with their $\lambda$ and $\mu$ in an attempt to show equality. Depends on both previous M's.
A1: Achieves (without errors) that they will intersect when $b=7$.
A1*: Cso States that when $b=7$, lines intersect and since lines are not parallel it shows that when $b\neq 7$ lines are skew.
To score the final mark there must be some statement that the lines intersect (or equivalent e.g. meet at a point, cross, etc.) when $b=7$ or that they do not intersect if $b\neq 7$ and that the lines are not parallel which may appear anywhere (reason not needed but may be present) so lines are skew when $b\neq 7$.
Ignore any work attempting to show that the lines are perpendicular or not.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Note that the previous 3 marks may be scored without explicitly seeing the values of both parameters e.g. $\mu=-\frac{11}{2}$, (2) $\to\lambda=3\mu+7\to4+5(3\mu+7)=-5+\mu b\to b=7$
- Alternative: M1: Uses $b=7$ and attempts to solve 2 equations to find either $\lambda$ or $\mu$ dM1: For attempting to solve 2 equations to find both $\lambda$ and $\mu$ Depends on the first M. A1: $\mu=-\frac{11}{2}$ and $\lambda=-\frac{19}{2}$ ddM1: Attempts to show that the 3rd equation is true for their values of $\lambda$ and $\mu$ Depends on both previous M's. A1: Achieves (without errors) that the 3rd equation gives the same values for (or equivalent) A1*: Cso States that when $b=7$, lines intersect and since lines are not parallel it shows that when $b\neq7$ lines are skew.
